index.title: MeshCore coverage and repeater signal · MeshCore Vitals
index.description: Check MeshCore coverage where you stand: repeaters in range, their signal (SNR), distance and direction. In your browser, over Bluetooth with your Companion.

companion.title: Companion battery and radio · MeshCore Vitals
companion.description: Check your MeshCore Companion over Bluetooth: battery, firmware, LoRa radio settings, noise floor, packets and airtime.

history.title: Coverage history · MeshCore Vitals
history.description: Look back at your last MeshCore sessions: coverage along your route and the repeaters heard, with their signal, on a map.

legal.description: Who publishes and hosts MeshCore Vitals, and what the app does with your data.

connect.hint: Turn your Companion on and keep it nearby before pairing.

landing.title: Your MeshCore coverage, live, wherever you stand.
landing.lead: Connect your Companion over Bluetooth and run a scan to see which repeaters hear you, and how well.
landing.install: No app to download: it all runs in your browser, on your phone or your computer.

map.alt: The app on a phone after a scan: the coverage, the repeaters on the map and their list.

list.title: The repeaters in range
list.text: After a scan, each repeater that heard you shows up with two readings, RX and TX. If it shares its position, you also see its direction, distance and altitude. The ones heard through another repeater are marked "via".
list.alt: The repeater list as the app shows it: Foxtrot and Juliett with a comfortable margin, Golf fair, Hotel tight, and Mike, relayed by Bravo.

rx.title: What you receive from it.
rx.text: The fuller the bar, the stronger the link.

tx.title: What it receives from you.
tx.text: Measured by the repeater during the scan.

bearing.title: Its direction.
bearing.text: On Android, the arrow turns with your phone.

detail.title: A repeater in detail
detail.text: Tap a repeater to see the signal both ways, the margin over the weakest signal your radio can decode, how reception changed since you connected, and the terrain between you.
detail.alt: A repeater's page on a phone: the margin gauge, the signal both ways and the reception chart of the session.

history.title: Your session history
history.text: Each connection with auto scan on is recorded as a session. The last {count} stay on your device, with the places you scanned from, the coverage at each scan and the best signal of each repeater.
history.alt: A session from the history on a phone: the scans on the map, the coverage over time and the repeaters heard.

companion.title: The state of your Companion
companion.text: The battery, the quality of the last signal received, the radio noise around you, the radio settings and the number of packets received and sent since boot.
companion.alt: The Companion page on a phone: battery, margin and noise floor, then the radio settings and the traffic.

autoScan.title: Automatic scans
autoScan.text: Turn it on for a new scan every minute while the page is open. Sessions are only kept with it on.

wakeLock.title: Screen kept on
wakeLock.text: Optionally keeps the screen on while you walk around, phone in hand.

terrain.title: Terrain profile
terrain.text: The ground between you and a repeater, with the Fresnel zone and adjustable antenna heights.

terrain.title: Terrain to the repeater
terrain.throttledHelp: Open-Meteo caps its free requests per minute, hour and day for each device. The profile comes back once the quota renews.

explain.marginal: The gap to the Fresnel zone is smaller than the uncertainty of the terrain (90 m cells) and of the positions. Trust the measured signal instead.
explain.clear: The terrain leaves the useful Fresnel zone clear. A weak signal would come from something else: buildings, trees, the antenna.
explain.partial: The ground stays below the line of sight but cuts into the Fresnel zone. Expect a few dB of loss, more in damp weather.
explain.blocked: A ridge rises above the line between you and the repeater. The signal only gets through by diffraction or reflection.

legal.title: Legal notice and privacy
legal.lead: The app has no account and no backend of its own: everything runs in your browser, and your sessions stay on your device.

analytics.title: Visit counts
analytics.text: Like any host, Vercel sees your IP address on each load. Visits are counted with Vercel Web Analytics, which sets no cookie. That service records the page, the referrer, the city and country guessed from your IP address, the browser, the OS and the device type, but never your radio or your GPS position. It does not keep your IP address: it tells visitors apart by a hash that changes daily.

services.title: Map and elevation
services.text: The app only contacts two other services, which also see your IP address. OpenFreeMap serves the map tiles, so it sees the areas the map shows. Open-Meteo gives the ground elevation for positions rounded to about 100 m: the repeaters', yours when the GPS gives no altitude, and the points along the path between you and a repeater whose terrain profile you open.

local.title: On your device
local.text: The session history, with your positions at each scan, stays in your browser and is never sent anywhere, like your settings. The only cookie keeps the language you pick for a year.

share.title: Shared images
share.text: A shared image only shows your position or your route if you turn on "Show my position" or "Show my route". The repeaters on it still show the area.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.text: This processing rests on the legitimate interest in running the site and counting its visits. The author keeps no data that identifies you: to erase everything, clear the site's data in your browser. For any question, open an issue on {github}. You can also complain to the CNIL, the French data protection authority.
